title: Classes & OOP
subtitle: class, __init__, self, inheritance, and dunder methods
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: As programs grow, related data and functions become hard to organise and reuse. A 'user' might have a name, email, and password — along with functions to validate them. Keeping all of this together needs structure.
whyItExists.solution: A class bundles data (attributes) and behaviour (methods) into a named type. You create objects (instances) from the class, each with their own data.
whyItExists.whenToUse: When you have data that belongs together with operations on that data. When you need multiple independent instances. When you want inheritance and polymorphism.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't use classes for simple utility functions or one-off scripts. A module with functions is often cleaner. For pure data containers, consider @dataclass.

explainModes.beginner: A class is a blueprint. A Car class describes what a car has (color, speed) and what it can do (accelerate, brake). Each real car you make from the blueprint (my_car = Car('red')) is an object with its own color and speed.
explainModes.simple: class Name: __init__(self, args) sets up each object. self refers to the current object. Methods are functions inside the class, always with self as first param. Inheritance: class Dog(Animal): inherits Animal's methods. super().__init__() calls parent's init. Special methods: __str__ for print(), __len__ for len().
explainModes.standard: Attributes set on self in __init__ are instance attributes (each object has its own). Class attributes (defined at class level) are shared across all instances — careful with mutable class attributes! @property creates computed read-only attributes. @classmethod receives the class (not instance) as first arg. @staticmethod is just a regular function inside the class namespace.
explainModes.technical: Python objects are dicts under the hood — instance.__dict__ stores instance attributes. Method Resolution Order (MRO) with C3 linearisation for multiple inheritance: ClassName.__mro__. Abstract base classes: from abc import ABC, abstractmethod. Dataclasses (@dataclass decorator) auto-generate __init__, __repr__, __eq__. __slots__ replaces instance dict with fixed slots (memory efficient). __getattr__/__setattr__/__delattr__ for attribute access control.
explainModes.deepDive: Python's object model: everything is an object, including classes themselves (metaclasses). type() is the default metaclass — type(MyClass) is type. Custom metaclasses with class Foo(metaclass=Meta) control class creation. Descriptors (__get__, __set__, __delete__) are what @property uses under the hood. __init_subclass__ runs when a class is subclassed. Protocols (typing.Protocol) for structural subtyping (duck typing + type hints).

content.code:
class BankAccount:
    # Class attribute — shared by all instances
    interest_rate = 0.05

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        # Instance attributes — unique to each object
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance += amount
        return self.balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise ValueError('Insufficient funds')
        self.balance -= amount
        return self.balance

    def __str__(self):
        return f'BankAccount({self.owner}: ₹{self.balance:,.2f})'

    def __repr__(self):
        return f'BankAccount(owner={self.owner!r}, balance={self.balance})'


# Create objects (instances)
acc1 = BankAccount('Prashant', 1000)
acc2 = BankAccount('Alice')         # balance defaults to 0

acc1.deposit(500)
acc1.withdraw(200)

print(acc1)            # BankAccount(Prashant: ₹1,300.00)
print(acc2.balance)    # 0
print(BankAccount.interest_rate)   # 0.05 (class attribute)

questions.question: What is self in a Python method?
options: A keyword like this in JavaScript
A reference to the class itself
A reference to the specific object the method was called on
An optional parameter you can rename to anything
questions.explanation: self is a reference to the instance (object) the method was called on. When you call acc.deposit(100), Python passes acc as the first argument (self). You CAN rename it — it's just a convention — but don't.

faq.q: What is the difference between __str__ and __repr__?
faq.a: __str__ is for human-readable output — what print() shows. __repr__ is for developer-readable output — what you see in the REPL or repr(). If only one is defined, __repr__ is used as fallback for both. Good __repr__ should ideally show how to recreate the object.

faq.q: When should I use @dataclass instead of a regular class?
faq.a: @dataclass is great when your class is primarily a data container. It auto-generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ based on field annotations. Use a regular class when you need custom __init__ logic, complex methods, or inheritance from non-dataclass bases.

examples: class User(Base): — SQLAlchemy ORM model inherits from Base
@dataclass class Config: — type-safe config with auto-generated init
class APIClient: — wraps requests session with auth, base URL, retry logic
